newsitem.title: CANADA: Vancouver bourse head says market mending its ways.
newsitem.headline: Vancouver bourse head says market mending its ways.

text.p: The head of Vancouver's scandal-plagued stock exchange said Tuesday that investors can have more confidence in the market after his first year on the job.
"There is no desire to tolerate unacceptable market practices and abuses," VSE president Michael Johnson said.

"I am pleased to report that during the past year we have made our mark in this area. The signs are clear that market behavior is being modified and new standards of conduct established. Recognizable change is evident and being reported by participants in our market," he said.
Johnson was speaking to a Vancouver business group. Asked after his speech to cite examples of the change, Johnson declined to be specific.

The British Columbia government has sought to strengthen regulation of the securities industry in the province and bolster investor confidence in the VSE, which has been dogged by allegation of fraud and abuse.

Johnson said the exchange was thriving, helped by its niche in bringing start-up mining exploration companies to market. In 1996, Vancouver-listed companies raised C$1.5 billion for mining exploration, a figure that Johnson said was one-quarter the world total.
In total, 50 new companies listed on the exchange and C$2.1 billion was raised while trading volume rose.
Johnson affirmed the exchange's commitment to focus on junior companies and said it had no ambitions to compete with senior markets like the Toronto Stock Exchange.
"We have become the world's leading venture capital market and in that role we will continue," he said.
Improving the efficiency of exchange operations is a major thrust and the VSE has sought to speed the handling of "well prepared" filings, Johnson said.
"We are also reviewing our policies as well as securities regulations to identify opportunities to prudently remove unnecessary policies," he said.
"We will then be consulting with the British Columbia Securities Commission as to inappropriate restrictiveness. Market competitiveness can be enhanced without compromising regulatory controls."

Speaking to reporters, Johnson refused to say which rules might be unnecessary. He said one area to be explored was to make policies on hold periods and escrow funds the same in both British Columbia and Alberta.
